text: Grain stores stand at {value} — thinner than I would like with winter ahead.
We have {value} Grain. Prayers will not refill a granary, whatever the Chaplain says.
The treasury holds {value} gold. Our obligations do not shrink to match.
There is talk in the villages, my lord. Unrest stands at {value} and climbs.
The levies grow soft. Quality stands at {value} — I would not march them far.
The pulpits grow cold toward us. The church's regard stands at {value}.
There are whispers about the crown itself, my lord. Best answered before they harden.
Ration the stores now. {tradeoff}
Commission a granary. {tradeoff}
Raise the rate a point. {tradeoff}
The church can spare a tithe. {tradeoff}
Ease the rate a point. {tradeoff}
Let the courts bite harder. {tradeoff}
An endowment would mend fences. {tradeoff}
Fresh levies, drilled hard. {tradeoff}

The new rate is cried in every market square.
The customs houses post the new tariff.
The muster rolls fill; sergeants curse recruits on every green.
The granary doors move to your word.
Word of your policy reaches every parish by Sunday.
The courts adjust their temper to yours.
Surveyors and masons are engaged; work begins.
Coin changes hands in quiet rooms.
The minister leans in and speaks freely.
The court takes careful note of your favour.
The rebuke lands before the whole court.
You speak privately; the rest of the council pretends not to notice.
Your word, kept. The court takes note.
A promise has lapsed unkept. The court remembers that too.
You accept them with thanks. Somewhere in the hall, someone decides you are the humble sort.
That night the court dines on goose, and the story grows fatter with each telling.
The farmer bows and withdraws. The geese, insulted, honk all the way home.
The books are turned inside out under a clerk's candle. Nothing incriminating surfaces — but the Steward will not soon forget being doubted in open council.
You let the matter drop. The cloak hangs a little heavier in the hall's memory than it should.
You praise the cut of the cloak before the whole court. The Steward preens; the tailors' bill, you notice, keeps growing.
You forbid the duel outright. Both men bow stiffly and say nothing more — which, from courtiers, is its own kind of complaint.
You let the duel proceed. Dawn comes, blood is drawn, pride is settled, and the court has a new story for winter nights.
You decree the matter be settled by wrestling, before the whole court, at noon. It is undignified, hilarious, and exactly the release the hall needed.
The parrot stays, perched on the Marshal's shoulder at every council since. The Spymaster mutters about loose tongues, feathered or otherwise.
The bird is delivered to the chapel as a curiosity for the scholars. The Chaplain is charmed; the Spymaster, relieved.
The parrot is quietly dispatched before it can repeat anything worse. The court mourns it more than seems entirely reasonable.
You hear her out on the spot. The reeve is fined and the widow leaves with what she is owed. The Chancellor says nothing, which says everything.
You send the matter through the proper channels. The Chancellor nods, satisfied; the widow's petition joins a very tall stack.
You have the reeve hanged by sundown, no trial required. The village cheers. The Chancellor does not.
Grain is bought abroad at a hard price. The granary fills; the treasury does not thank you for it.
Rations are cut through the coming winter. The granary holds; the villages grumble.
The church opens its stores, this once. The Chaplain's smile does not quite reach his eyes — this favor will be called in.
Patrols go out along the coast road. The merchants are grateful, and pay their tolls a little more cheerfully for a season.
You raise the tariff to fund the patrols. The irony is not lost on anyone — least of all the smugglers, who have never been busier.
You hire the bandits as toll-keepers. It is shameless, it is cheap, and it works exactly as well as the Spymaster predicted.
The calf is burned publicly, per the old custom. The Chaplain leads the rite himself; the scholars, elsewhere, only sigh.
The calf is crated and sent to the capital's scholars. The Chaplain calls it an omen indulged; the learned call it a fine specimen.
You have the calf served at your own table, in full view of the court, to show what you think of omens. Half the hall is scandalized. The other half asks for seconds.
A full inquiry turns the works budget inside out. Someone's hand is found in the till; the coin is clawed back, at some cost to the Steward's pride.
You rebuild quietly and ask no questions. The court is relieved. Somewhere, a ledger is quietly rewritten again.
The builder is made to pay for it himself, no trial required. It is cheap and it is unjust, and the guild will remember both.
The prophet is arrested at dawn. The crowds scatter, muttering, and do not entirely forget.
You let him preach. The grumbling in the market towns gains a voice, and voices, left alone, gather others.
You go to the market square yourself and answer him, sermon for sermon, before the whole crowd. It is a gamble that pays — for now, they are yours again.
You claim the cargo in full. The treasury is glad of it; the merchant's ruin is a story that travels with foreign ships for a season.
You return the cargo, salvage rights and all. The merchant leaves in disbelief, already speaking of you to every captain he knows.
You keep half as a salvage fee and let him take the rest. Nobody leaves entirely satisfied, and nobody leaves entirely wronged.
You claim the mine for the crown outright. The treasury swells; the nobility takes careful, silent note.
You split the proceeds with the landholder. Nobody is thrilled, but nobody is ruined, and the court watches how you treat your own.
You waive the crown's share entirely. The landholder is stunned, then grateful — the kind of debt that outlasts a single favor.
You have the treatise suppressed. The Chaplain says nothing about it again, which is its own kind of answer.
You endorse the treatise publicly. The Chaplain is quietly, deeply moved. The hierarchy takes careful notes.
You laugh it off over dinner and change the subject. The manuscript keeps circulating all the same, seminary to seminary.
You arrange the match. The treasury fills; the nobility watches, unamused, as blood and coin change hands together.
You decline, gracefully. Nothing is lost — except, perhaps, the magnate's good opinion of your court's ambition.
You counter-offer a lesser cousin instead. Half the dowry arrives, along with a tenth of the outrage.
You have the actor punished. The act does not stop. It simply moves underground, and grows sharper for the effort.
You ignore it entirely. Within a season it has become less mockery than fond legend — a story the realm tells about itself.
You hire him outright for the ceremonies you cannot stand. He is, by every account, better at them than you ever were.
You call the court to vigil. Candles burn through the night; the Chaplain leads, and for once the whole hall is quiet together.
You commission the scholars to chart its course instead. The Chaplain mutters about faithlessness; the astronomers are delighted.
You say nothing and let the comet pass unremarked. The court's predictions are quietly recorded — and quietly remembered.
You stand your ground and take the charge yourself. It is over in a heartbeat, and the Marshal will be telling this story for years.
You let the huntsmen do their work. A quick-thinking courtier puts himself between you and the boar — a debt you will not forget.
You skipped the hunt entirely, for paperwork. You were never in danger. The court jokes about it for a full season.
You pay the debt in full. The treasury groans, but your credit — and your name — stays good.
The Steward talks the agent into new terms. The interest climbs, but the crisis, for now, is deferred.
You default outright. The gold stays in your coffers; the lender's family will not forget it. The Steward puts his head in his hands.
You take the child as a ward. The court murmurs. Whatever he becomes, he becomes it at your table, under your eye.
You leave him to the monastery, watched. It is safe, and it is cold, and everyone tells you it was the wise choice.
You send the child abroad. The problem leaves with him. The story of him does not.
You hold the feast in full. The jester issues one real mock-decree from the throne, and the hall roars with it long after the wine runs out.
You hold the feast, but keep your own seat. It misses the point somewhat, and the court quietly agrees.
You cancel the custom outright. The Chancellor is delighted. Everyone else composes a very memorable couplet about you.
Very well — ration the stores. See it done gently.
Commission the granary. The realm eats tomorrow because we build today.
Raise the rate. I will bear the grumbling.
Take the tithe. The church can spare it this season.
Ease the rate. Let the villages breathe.
Let the courts bite harder, then. Order first.
Make the endowment. Grace is worth gold.
Raise the levies. Drill them well.
Send your whisperers. Quietly.
Build the road. Trade must move.

The herald coughs. "None you address are present, my lord."
